books.section: The Rise of the Service Sector
Prosperity and a New World Order (1988–2000)

stem: The chart best supports which conclusion about the American economy after 1970?

options.text: The economy shifted from making goods to providing services
The United States stopped producing manufactured goods
options.misconception: Background: factory output kept growing; only the share of jobs in factories fell.

options.text: Factory wages rose because factory jobs became scarce
options.misconception: The chart says nothing about wages. Background: many displaced factory workers moved into lower-paid service work.
The chart shows a steady forty-year slide, not a sudden stop after one new rule.

rationales.A: Background: as factory jobs shrank, service jobs in retail, health care, and finance grew to take their place.
rationales.B: Background: the United States kept producing more manufactured goods; what fell was the share of workers making them.
rationales.C: The chart tracks jobs, not pay. Background: many former factory workers moved into lower-paid service jobs.
rationales.D: A forty-year slide needs a long cause. Background: automation, trade, and offshoring all pushed the same way.
rationales.general:
1. Picture the whole workforce as a pie: the factory slice shrank from a quarter to less than a tenth.
2. Ask where the workers went. Background: service jobs in retail, health care, and finance grew as factory jobs shrank.
3. Do not overread the chart: it shows jobs, not output, and output kept growing.
4. The steady slide points to deep forces, not one event.
Remember: the economy did not stop making things — it stopped employing so many people to make them.
